answer:
# **Two Skies, One Heart**

### *A Story of Masks, Courage, and the Space Between Stars*

---

## Part One: Ordinary Days

The alarm clock on Marcus Webb's nightstand had been broken for three weeks.

It didn't matter. He always woke up before it anyway — a habit born from years of early morning basketball practice, a routine that had survived even after he'd quit the team last spring. He lay there in the gray September light, staring at the water stain on his ceiling that looked vaguely like a running wolf, and thought about nothing in particular for exactly four minutes before swinging his legs over the side of the bed.

Marcus was seventeen. He was the kind of person who existed comfortably in the middle of things — not the most popular kid at Lakewood High, not the least popular either. He had a small, solid group of friends, decent grades in the subjects he actually cared about, and a reputation for being quietly funny in a way that sneaked up on people. He had dark hair that curled slightly at his temples when it got too long, which it always did because he kept forgetting to get it cut. His mother said he had his father's eyes — a warm, light brown that turned almost amber in direct sunlight — though Marcus didn't think about his father's eyes very much at all.

He pulled on a gray hoodie, dark jeans, and his beat-up white sneakers, grabbed the backpack that had been leaning against his desk since Friday night, and headed downstairs.

His mother, Diane Webb, was already at the kitchen counter with her second cup of coffee, laptop open to what Marcus assumed were lesson plans. She taught seventh-grade English at a middle school across town. She was a small, sharp-featured woman with reading glasses perpetually pushed up on her forehead and an almost supernatural ability to sense when something was bothering him.

"There's oatmeal," she said without looking up.

"I see it," Marcus said.

"And there's fruit."

"Mom."

"I'm just saying fruit exists and is available in this kitchen."

He ate the oatmeal standing up, rinsed the bowl, kissed his mother on the top of her head, and walked out into the cool September morning.

---

Lakewood was a mid-sized city in that particular American way — big enough to have a skyline with a few buildings that actually qualified as tall, small enough that everyone still complained there was nothing to do. It sat in a wide valley between two gentle mountain ridges, and on clear mornings you could see both ridges from the right spots, deep blue and hazy, like suggestions of something larger beyond.

Marcus walked twelve blocks to school, which he preferred to taking the bus. The walk gave him time to listen to music and exist in his own head without anyone talking to him. This was not because he disliked people. It was because he had learned, gradually, that he needed those pockets of quiet to function properly.

Lakewood High was a three-story brick building that had been built in 1962 and renovated badly in 1994, resulting in a confusing architectural personality — brutalist bones dressed up in cheerful pastel trim that had long since faded. There were seven hundred and forty students enrolled. Marcus knew maybe sixty of them by name.

He arrived at his locker — number 247, second floor, east hallway — at 7:52, eight minutes before the first bell. He was spinning the combination when he heard the soft collision of a backpack against the locker directly beside his, number 248.

He glanced over.

The girl standing there was, he had long since decided, one of the most puzzling people he'd ever been in proximity to.

Her name was Kara Danvers.

She had been a student at Lakewood High for two years, having transferred in at the start of sophomore year from somewhere that she'd never been entirely specific about. She was tall — nearly as tall as Marcus, which was not nothing, since Marcus was six feet even — with long blond hair that she usually wore pulled back somewhat haphazardly, as though she'd put it up in a hurry and hadn't revisited the decision. She had blue eyes of a shade that Marcus had noticed, involuntarily, on exactly one occasion and had spent subsequent weeks not thinking about. She wore unremarkable clothes — jeans, plain sweaters, the occasional flannel — with the slightly distracted air of someone who had put them on while thinking about something else entirely.

By any objective measure, Kara Danvers was pretty. This was not the puzzling part.

The puzzling part was everything else.

She was, academically, somewhere between brilliant and alien. She had a habit of answering questions in AP Physics with a casual precision that made their teacher, Mr. Okonkwo, occasionally pause and blink before writing her response on the board. In AP History she'd once corrected a detail in the textbook about the construction of the Panama Canal in a way that was completely specific and completely correct, verified by Mr. Okonkwo's subsequent fifteen minutes of frantic Googling. She read constantly — not just assigned reading, but actual books she seemed to have chosen herself, ranging from astrophysics to Greek mythology to what appeared, one memorable Thursday, to be a Sumerian language primer.

And yet, socially, she was almost completely invisible.

Not in a tragic way, exactly. She wasn't bullied or excluded in any dramatic sense. She was just... quiet. Excessively, almost unnaturally quiet. She sat at the edge of lunch tables, contributed to class discussions only when directly called upon, moved through the hallways with her eyes slightly downcast and her headphones in one ear, as if she were trying to take up the minimum possible amount of space in the world. She had, as far as Marcus could tell, exactly one friend — a girl named Becca Torres who was in the drama club and talked enough for both of them.

Marcus had locker 247. Kara had locker 248. They had been adjacent since the beginning of junior year, which was now three weeks in, and their relationship so far consisted entirely of the sort of micro-interactions that barely qualified as communication.

*Hey.*

*Hey.*

*Do you have the calc homework?*

*Yeah, here.*

That was more or less the full archive of their personal history.

This morning, she was fumbling with her combination — she always seemed to have trouble with it, which Marcus found mildly baffling given the Panama Canal thing — while balancing a stack of three books in her opposite arm. One of the books was, he noted, a collection of essays on orbital mechanics. The other two were history texts. The third was a battered paperback of *Rebecca* by Daphne du Maurier that seemed to be in the middle of being destroyed and rebuilt simultaneously, its spine cracked and its pages furred with use.

"You're going to drop those," Marcus said.

He hadn't entirely planned to say it. It just happened.

Kara looked at him. There was a moment in which she seemed genuinely startled, as though she'd forgotten he existed between the end of Friday's school day and now.

"I'm fine," she said, in a voice that was quiet and slightly careful, the way she always spoke. 

Two seconds later, the orbital mechanics book slid off the top of the stack.

Marcus caught it.

It was a reflex, the kind that came from years of basketball, and it happened so fast that for a moment they both just looked at the book in his hand.

"Thanks," Kara said.

"Sure." He handed it back. "You might want to put those in the locker before you add more."

"I know how lockers work," she said, in a tone that was not quite sharp — more like the idea of sharp, slightly muffled.

"I didn't say you didn't. I just—"

"I'm fine," she repeated, and turned back to her locker, which had finally opened.

Marcus watched her for a half-second longer than was probably necessary, then turned back to his own locker and began pulling out his own things.

*She's strange*, he thought. Not unkindly. Just observationally.

He had thought this before.

He would think it many more times before he understood what it meant.

---

## Part Two: The Shape of Her Secret

What Marcus Webb did not know, could not know, had no framework for even beginning to suspect, was this:

Kara Danvers was not from Lakewood.

She was not from anywhere in the continental United States. She was not from anywhere on Earth. She was not, in the precise technical sense of the word, human — although she was close enough that the distinction barely registered in daily life, except in the specific ways that it registered enormously.

Her name — her real name, the one that existed before the name Danvers — was Kara Zor-El. She had been born on a planet called Krypton, in a city called Argo, to a scientist named Zor-El and a judge named Alura. She had grown up in a world of extraordinary technological sophistication, of crystalline architecture and advanced science and a culture that had, in certain ways, been more developed than Earth's by several thousand years.

She had also been twelve years old when that world ended.

The details of what had happened to Krypton were not something Kara spent a great deal of time thinking about. She had learned, with time and with the help of the family she'd found on Earth — primarily her adoptive parents, Jeremiah and Eliza Danvers, and her adoptive sister Alex — to store the memory in a place that was not exactly forgotten but not constantly present either. A sealed room. A weight carried not in the hands but distributed across the whole body, so evenly that you could almost forget it was there.

She was, on Earth, under a yellow sun, something extraordinary.

She was, by any reasonable measure, the most powerful person on the planet.

She could fly — not metaphorically, not in a plane, but actually, personally fly, rising from the ground and moving through the air at speeds that could rival jets, her cape streaming behind her, the entire world spread below her like a map of everything that still existed and still mattered. She was strong in a way that required new vocabulary — she had, once, very carefully, moved a shipping freighter off a reef without breaking a sweat. She had heat vision, a focused beam of thermal energy that could ignite steel. She had freeze breath, a cold exhalation precise enough to seal a broken dam. She could hear sounds from miles away — individual heartbeats in a crowd, a whispered conversation through three concrete walls, the specific frequency of distress in a person's voice. She could see through objects, see the internal architecture of things, the hidden scaffolding of the world. She was, for all practical purposes, invulnerable — the only significant exception being a greenish mineral called Kryptonite, fragments of her destroyed home world, which could reduce her, rapidly and terrifyingly, to something closer to human.

She had been using these abilities, carefully and secretly and with the constant support of her sister Alex and a small government organization called the DEO, to help people for two years. She was known to the people of Lakewood, and to the wider world, as Supergirl.

The name had started as a headline — *Girl of Steel Saves Bridge Collapse Victims, All 23 Passengers Safe* — and had stuck the way good names do, through repetition and resonance. She had not chosen it. She had decided, eventually, that she liked it anyway.

As Supergirl, she wore a costume that her mother — a memory of her mother, preserved in Kryptonian crystal — had helped her design: a blue suit with the House of El crest on the chest, a red skirt, red boots, and a red cape that moved in a way that was difficult to describe except as having its own intention, as though it knew where it was going. Her hair was down and loose. She stood at her full height. She did not look at the ground.

As Kara Danvers, she wore her hair up, her clothes quiet, her expression carefully controlled. She spoke softly. She moved carefully. She had, over two years of practice, developed an extraordinary ability to seem unremarkable.

This was, she had explained once to her sister, not about deception.

"It's about protection," she had said. "For them. If people knew who I was — if someone who wanted to hurt me knew who I was — everyone around me would be in danger."

"I know," Alex had said. "I know, Kara. I'm just saying — you don't have to be *that* invisible."

"It's easier this way."

"Easier isn't always better."

Kara had thought about this. She still thought about it sometimes, in the moments between things.

The truth was more complicated than protection, though protection was real and true. The truth was also that existing as a human being — as someone unremarkable, someone navigating the ordinary complexity of high school and homework and the social cartography of a lunch cafeteria — felt like an important thing to practice. Like something she owed herself. She had missed so much. She wanted to know what it felt like to be simply *in the world* without the weight of responsibility, without the constant vigilance, even for the short hours that school required.

She was not good at it yet. She was not sure she would ever be fully good at it.

But she kept practicing.

---

The thing about having superhuman senses at school was that it was almost entirely a liability.

The sound level of a high school cafeteria, experienced through hearing that could distinguish between seven hundred heartbeats, was essentially an act of auditory violence. Kara had developed techniques — a kind of mental focusing, a tightening down of the bandwidth — that made it manageable, but it required constant effort. This was, in large part, why she always seemed slightly distracted. She was, in fact, extremely attentive. She was just attending to many things simultaneously, most of which were invisible to everyone around her.

She could hear, right now, the conversation at the table three rows away where Tyler Marsh was telling his friends about a party on Saturday. She could hear the lunch supervisor's phone buzzing in his pocket. She could hear, faintly and from somewhere outside the building, the specific pitch of a car alarm on Clement Street that had been going off, ignored, for eleven minutes.

She could hear Marcus Webb, two seats down and across the table, saying something quietly funny to his friend Danny Cho that made Danny laugh with his mouth full, which produced a sound that was both gross and genuinely cheerful.

She looked up, involuntarily, in his direction.

He wasn't looking at her. He was leaning back in his chair, grinning at something Danny had said in response, one arm thrown over the empty chair beside him. He had a habit, she had noticed, of occupying space comfortably — not in a loud or aggressive way, but with a kind of easy physical presence that suggested he had made peace with taking up room in the world.

She looked back at her food.

She had not told anyone at school — not Becca, not any teacher, no one — who she really was. The secret was necessary. She understood this. She had understood it since she was twelve years old and her cousin, Clark, who had been on Earth since infancy and who had built his own human life with far more practice than she'd had, had sat with her in the Danvers' kitchen and explained, carefully, why the secret mattered.

She still sometimes wished she could just *tell* someone.

Not to impress them. Not for the relief of being known in the full sense. Just to explain why she sometimes went distant in the middle of conversations, why she occasionally had to excuse herself quickly and without explanation from places, why she sometimes looked at the sky when she thought no one was watching with an expression that she couldn't fully conceal — something between longing and belonging, something that didn't have a human word for it.

She finished her lunch alone, as usual, because Becca had a rehearsal thing and the rest of the table had drifted off in groups. She picked up her tray. She walked past Marcus and Danny's table.

"Hey," Marcus said.

She paused. "Hey."

"You're in AP History, right? Period four?"

"Yes."

"Do you have the reading for Thursday? The one about the Marshall Plan? I think I wrote down the wrong pages."

"It's 287 through 310," she said, and then, because his eyebrows went up slightly: "I checked it twice because I wasn't sure either."

She had not checked it twice. She had heard the assignment from across the room with complete accuracy while simultaneously tracking a heated argument between two freshmen by the lockers and monitoring a weather pattern that she'd been watching develop over the eastern ridge because it had the particular signature of a storm system that could cause flooding.

"Cool," he said. "Thanks."

"Sure," she said.

She put her tray away and left the cafeteria.

## Part Three: The Bridge

It happened on a Tuesday.

Marcus was walking home from school — the long way, because he wasn't in a hurry, because the light at 4 in the afternoon in September had a particular quality that he liked, golden and slightly sleepy — when he heard the sirens.

Not one siren. Many sirens, converging, overlapping, the particular audio texture of something serious happening somewhere close. He stopped at the corner of Fifth and Morrison and stood there for a moment, listening, trying to determine direction.

He could see, over the rooftops to the west, a thin column of black smoke.

He knew, with the immediate certainty of someone who had grown up in this city, what was to the west. The Lakewood Suspension Bridge. A hundred-year-old structure that crossed the wide part of the Calloway River, connecting downtown to the older residential neighborhoods on the west bank. He'd walked it a hundred times. Driven over it with his mother. He knew the particular rhythm of its wood-and-metal walkway under his feet.

He started moving toward it, because he was seventeen and curious and because something about the smoke made a cold wire of anxiety run through him.

By the time he got close enough to see, there was already a crowd. Fire trucks and police cars and ambulances had created a perimeter on the near end, their lights casting alternating red and blue across the pale faces of the gathering onlookers. Marcus pushed through to a spot near the railing of the riverside walkway where he could get a clear line of sight.

The bridge was in crisis.

He didn't know what had started it — an accident, a structural failure, something else — but the eastern tower of the suspension system had partially collapsed. The roadway had cracked down the middle, and a section of perhaps forty feet had torn free and was hanging at a violent angle over the river, held by the remaining cables, swinging slowly. There were cars on that section — three of them, he could count them — their drivers trapped inside, visible through the windshields as small pale shapes, their hands against the glass.

He heard the sound of the crowd around him shift.

Something had changed in the air. Not a sound, exactly, but a displacement — a pressure change, a movement of air in a direction that made no physical sense, coming from above.

He looked up.

She came out of the sky like a comet deciding to be careful.

He would try to describe it later — to Danny, to himself in the private narrative of his own head — and find that language was not quite up to the task. She was moving fast, very fast, and then she wasn't, decelerating with a precision that shouldn't have been possible, and the red cape was a banner behind her and the last of the afternoon sun caught the gold of her hair and the silver of the El crest on her chest, and she landed — if landing was even the right word, if that gentle, controlled descent to the cracked roadway of the bridge deserved a word that pedestrian — with a sound like a very quiet exhale.

Supergirl.

Marcus had seen footage. Everyone had seen footage — phone videos, news camera clips, the grainy satellite images that had made their way to the front pages. But footage was not the same as this. Footage was a thing happening in a screen. This was a thing happening in the actual world, fifty meters away, visible to his actual eyes.

She was *real* in a way that footage had not prepared him for.

She moved immediately. She crossed the cracked section of roadway in three long strides, assessed the hanging section with a visual sweep that lasted less than a second, and then did something that made the crowd around Marcus produce a collective, involuntary sound — a sharp intake of breath, a low murmur of disbelief. She crouched, found two of the thickest suspension cables that had torn free, and took one in each hand, and held them.

Just held them.

The hanging section of the bridge — the section with three cars and what turned out to be seven people, as Marcus would learn from the news later — stopped swinging. Stopped moving. Was held in place by the girl in the blue suit, her feet planted, her arms extended, the cables taut in her grip.

"Emergency services are coming," she called out, toward the hanging section, and her voice was clear and calm and carried across the noise of the wind and the distant sirens like something projected. "I've got you. You're not going anywhere. Just stay still and keep calm."

There was something in the voice that Marcus could not identify exactly. Not just confidence — though it was confident, completely, without a single note of performance in it. Something underneath the confidence. Something that said: *I know what it is to be afraid, and I am telling you that right now, fear is not necessary. I am here.*

He stood very still on the walkway.

He could not look away.

The next twenty minutes were — and he would think about this word later, would decide it was exactly right — *extraordinary*. She held those cables while the emergency crews brought in reinforcement rigging from the fire trucks. She held them through the wind that picked up off the river, through the noise, through the logistical complexity of getting all seven people off the hanging section safely. She held them with a steadiness that was not human in any way he had words for, but which did not feel alien. It felt, somehow, deeply and specifically *good*. Like the opposite of disaster.

When the last person — a small boy, maybe six years old, in a red jacket — was lifted off the section by a harness lowered from a fire truck crane, and the boy reached the safe part of the roadway and ran immediately to a woman who must have been his mother, and the woman held the boy with the particular intensity of someone who has almost lost what they can least afford to lose, Marcus felt something happen in his chest that he did not have immediate vocabulary for.

He looked at Supergirl.

She had released the cables. The engineers had secured the section with the emergency rigging. She stood on the cracked roadway and watched the mother and the small boy, and even from fifty meters away, Marcus could see her expression.

She was smiling.

Not a grand smile. Not a triumphant, headline-ready smile. A small, genuine, deeply private smile — the kind you make when something that was broken is suddenly okay, when the worst thing doesn't happen, when the world decides to be kind.

She turned and looked at the crowd on the walkway.

For a moment — and Marcus would be unable to explain this, would attribute it to adrenaline or the quality of the light or simple projection — it seemed like she looked directly at him. Her eyes, at this distance, were impossible to read. But the look lasted one second, maybe two, and then she looked away, and she rose from the roadway without effort, without drama, straight up into the sky, and was gone.

The crowd released the breath it had been collectively holding.

Marcus released his.

He stood there for a long time after.

## Part Four: New Orbit

He became slightly obsessed. He would admit this, privately and honestly, without significant embarrassment. It was not, he was careful to tell himself, a crush in the conventional sense. It was more like — a sustained astonishment. An inability to stop thinking about the specific quality of what he had witnessed. The calibration of it.

He read everything published about Supergirl. Which was quite a lot and also, he noted, almost entirely useless. The articles tended to focus on the scale of her abilities — the weight she could lift, the speed she could achieve, the catalog of disasters she had intervened in — and almost never on the thing that had actually struck him, which was the *manner* of what she did. The smallness and specificity of it alongside the obvious enormousness. The way she'd spoken to the people on the bridge. The quality of that smile.

He talked about it with Danny, who listened with good humor for approximately eight minutes before saying, "Dude, are you in love with Supergirl?"

"That's not what this is," Marcus said.

"What is it then?"

He struggled for a moment. "It's more like — when you see someone do something really well. Like, masterfully. And you can't stop thinking about the thing they did."

Danny considered this. "Like watching Steph Curry shoot?"

"Sort of. Except bigger."

"Bigger than Steph Curry."

"I'm trying to explain something."

"Okay, okay." Danny ate a chip. "I saw the footage from the bridge. It was pretty nuts."

"Footage isn't the same."

"You keep saying that."

"Because it's true."

He kept reading, watching, thinking. He found a series of accounts from people who'd been helped by Supergirl — a personal essay by the engineer who'd been rescued from the collapsed building in April, a social media thread from a family whose house fire she'd extinguished, a piece in the Lakewood Gazette by a woman who'd been pulled from her sinking car in the Calloway flood last spring. They all described different versions of the same thing: the way she made you feel safe not because of what she could do but because of *how she was*. The presence of her. The certainty.

He thought about that smile, the private one, the one she didn't know he'd seen.

---

The following Friday, he was late to AP History — not by much, just thirty seconds past the bell, because he'd stopped to help a freshman whose combination lock had jammed — and as he slipped into the room, the only open seat was one up from his usual spot, which meant he ended up sitting directly next to Kara Danvers.

She glanced at him briefly when he sat down.

He opened his notebook.

Mr. Okonkwo was in the middle of a discussion about the Korean War's effect on domestic U.S. policy, and he threw a question to the class: "Can anyone tell me why the Truman administration was reluctant to escalate in Korea in ways that might have militarily shortened the conflict?"

Silence, the way there always was when the question had too many parts.

Marcus was thinking about it — he actually knew this one, had read about it — but before he could raise his hand, Kara spoke.

"Because escalation risked Soviet intervention," she said. Her voice was quiet, but there was no hesitation in it. "And the administration had just watched China enter the conflict when General MacArthur pushed too close to the Yalu River. They'd already seen what happened when a regional conflict got pulled into the orbit of a superpower. Truman was trying to fight a limited war in an era when the concept of a 'limited war' was still being invented."

Mr. Okonkwo wrote *limited war* on the board with evident satisfaction. "Excellent. Who can add to that?"

Marcus looked at Kara.

She had gone back to her notebook, writing something in the careful, slightly cramped hand he'd noticed before. She didn't look up.

He thought, for some reason, of the way Supergirl had assessed the bridge in that one-second sweep — the rapid, total comprehension of a complex situation, the immediate isolation of what mattered.

He pushed the thought away. It was a coincidence of impression. Smart girl. Capable hero. The world was full of capable people. They were not the same person.

He turned back to his own notes.

After class, they both ended up at the door at the same time.

"You've read about the Korean War a lot," Marcus said. He said it conversationally, without an agenda.

Kara seemed slightly surprised that he was addressing her. "I read about a lot of things," she said.

"Orbital mechanics. Marshall Plan. Korea. Are you deciding what to major in?"

Something shifted in her expression — almost a smile, not quite reaching the surface. "I like knowing things," she said, simply.

"Fair enough," he said.

They went their separate ways.

But he thought about that for the rest of the day. *I like knowing things.* The absolute simplicity of it. The way it hadn't been a defense or a performance. Just a true statement, offered plainly.

## Part Five: Frequencies

Three weeks after the bridge.

Marcus was sitting on the roof of his house — there was a flat section over the back porch that he accessed through his bedroom window, a private space he used for the specific activity of existing without being talked to — with his notebook and his phone, not really working on anything, when he heard it.

A sound.

High and fast and then gone, like something breaking the surface of the air and then sealing it back up behind itself.

He looked up.

He couldn't see anything. The sky was dark-blue with the last light of dusk, the first stars faintly visible. Whatever had made the sound was gone.

But he sat there for a long time afterward, looking at the sky.

---

Meanwhile.

Three miles away, moving fast and high and invisible to anyone not specifically looking for her, Kara was finishing a loop.

She did this every evening she could manage it — a patrol circuit over Lakewood, wide and methodical, listening on all frequencies, watching with eyes that could see everything and register it and react. Most evenings it was nothing. The ordinary texture of a city's distress: fender benders, medical incidents, the ordinary grief of daily life that didn't require a girl from Krypton to resolve. Every few days there was something real — a fire, a structural emergency, a situation involving violence that the police needed a second of intervention to safely conclude.

Tonight it was nothing. Which was, she had learned, a kind of good.

She arced back east, adjusting her heading slightly, and from a thousand feet above the residential grid she let her hearing drift, almost idle — not focused, not searching, just open.

She passed over her own street. She could hear, as she always could, the familiar sounds of the Danvers house: Eliza's radio in the kitchen, the particular creak of the third stair from the bottom. She could hear Becca Torres, two streets over, rehearsing lines in her bedroom, getting a particular speech wrong and starting over.

She kept moving.

She was over the eastern residential grid when she caught something new. Not a distress signal. Just a sound.

Music.

Someone was playing guitar. On a roof, which was why it was audible without interference — no walls, no ceiling, just the open air. Acoustic guitar, and the person playing was not in any sense professional but was not casual either; they played with focus, returning to a difficult chord transition again and again until they got it clean.

She found herself slowing down involuntarily.

She floated, barely moving, at three hundred feet, and listened.

Then she used the other vision — let her gaze sharpen and descend, telescoping through the dark to the flat roof section over a back porch — and she saw who it was.

Marcus Webb.

He was sitting with his back against the chimney stack, a battered acoustic guitar in his hands, his notebook open beside him, playing the same transition over and over. His expression was the focused, private one — the one she'd seen on him occasionally in class, when he was working on something he actually cared about. He didn't know anyone was watching. He didn't know anyone could see him from here. He was just a boy on a roof in the dark, playing guitar badly and then gradually better.

She watched for a moment longer than she should have.

Then she moved on, because she was Supergirl and Supergirl had a city to watch and did not hover above her classmates' houses, observing them.

But the transition he'd finally gotten clean stayed with her, playing back, all the way home.

---

## Part Six: Gravity

October.

The encounter happened because of rain.

It had been raining since three in the afternoon, the kind of serious October rain that had no sense of proportion — heavy and cold and wind-driven, the sort of weather that made the city feel slightly hostile, like it was reminding everyone who was really in charge. By seven in the evening it had developed into something more concerning: the storm system that Kara had been tracking for a week was exactly as problematic as she'd expected, and the Calloway River, swelled by the rain, was cresting toward the flood markers.

She'd been monitoring it all afternoon between homework and dinner. At 7:15, her phone received the alert that the city issued for the low-lying area on the river's eastern bank — *Evacuation advisory, Zones 4 and 5, residents should move to higher ground immediately*. At 7:23, as she was already pulling on the suit, her DEO contact radioed to confirm what she already knew: the secondary levee at the Miller Street crossing was showing stress fractures and needed intervention.

She was in the air at 7:24.

The rain at altitude was spectacular in a purely aesthetic sense, if you weren't the one the rain was happening to — the city lights below fractured and multiplied in every drop, turning the sky into a moving chandelier. She registered this and filed it away and focused on the levee.

The Miller Street levee was a concrete-and-earthwork barrier about forty meters long, built in the 1980s as a supplement to the main river wall. The fractures she'd been warned about were real and progressing: she could see them with her penetrating vision before she landed, hairline cracks spreading from a foundational weak point, water beginning to push through. If the levee failed, two streets of residential buildings would take several feet of water within minutes.

She landed on top of the levee in the rain, found the primary stress point, and went to work.

She spent forty minutes there. It was not dramatic, as these things went — no one to rescue, no cameras (though later she knew someone would have gotten footage from a nearby window, there was always footage), just the technical problem of reinforcing a failing structure with the physical materials available and the abilities she had. She packed the fractures with the loosened earthwork, used her freeze breath to seal the more critical points, used her strength to push the concrete sections back into alignment and hold them there while the emergency engineering crew arrived with their quick-setting compound.

She did not particularly enjoy this kind of work in the sense of finding it exciting. She did it because it needed to be done and she was the one who could do it. There was a satisfaction in that — a quieter, more durable satisfaction than the adrenaline of a dramatic rescue.

When it was done, and the crew chief had given her a thumbs-up, she turned to leave.

And found, because Lakewood was not a large city and the paths people took were not infinite, Marcus Webb standing on the sidewalk at the edge of the emergency barrier tape, completely soaked, watching her.

He had apparently been there for some of it at least. He was in a dark jacket with the hood up, hands in his pockets, the rain plastering his curling hair flat, and he was looking at her with an expression she didn't immediately have a category for. It was not the usual civilian response — not fear, not screaming awe, not the phone-out-for-footage reflex. He was just looking at her. Very steadily.

She walked toward him because the emergency tape ended near where he was standing and it was the natural direction, not for any other reason.

"Are you from this area?" she asked, because that was what she would have asked anyone — she needed to know if he lived in the evacuated zone. Her voice, when she was Supergirl, was slightly different than Kara Danvers's voice. A fraction fuller. Less careful.

"No," he said. "I was running. Got caught in the rain, came this way, and then—" He gestured at the levee behind her.

"You should get inside," she said.

"I know." He didn't move. "The bridge. I was there. Three weeks ago."

She looked at him. The rain was very loud on the pavement. "I remember," she said, which was true. She remembered all of them — not always the faces in detail, but the shape of each moment, the specific weight of it.

"I wanted to say — I mean, I know you probably hear this a lot." He stopped. Seemed to recalibrate. "I was watching. The whole time. And I wanted to say that the *way* you did it — it wasn't just— it was the way you talked to them. To the people in the cars. The way you said—" He paused again, searching. "*I've got you.*"

She waited.

"That was the thing," he said. "Not the cables. Not the holding. Just those three words and the way you said them. It changed the air."

She was quiet for a moment.

She was used to thanks. She was used to public gratitude and civic commendations and the specific generosity of people who needed to express their relief. She was not used to this. Not used to someone standing in the rain and telling her the specific true thing about what had mattered.

"Thank you," she said, and her voice was slightly different on those two words, slightly less formal. "Most people mention the cables."

"The cables were impressive," he said, with a small gravity in his voice that she recognized, after a second, as his sense of humor — the dry, sneaking kind. The kind she'd noticed in class. "I'm not minimizing the cables."

She almost — almost — laughed.

"What's your name?" she asked.

"Marcus," he said. "Marcus Webb."

"You should really go inside, Marcus Webb. You're going to get hypothermia."

"I know." He still didn't move, for one more moment. "I'm going. I just — thank you. For this." He gestured again, at the levee, at the whole wet night. "For all of it."

She looked at him in the rain. She catalogued his face, the detail of it, filed it alongside the memory of guitar music from a roof at dusk.

"Take care of yourself," she said.

She rose into the rain, and was gone.

---

He stood there until he couldn't see her anymore.

Then he went home, changed his soaked clothes, and sat at his desk, and thought about the way she'd said *most people mention the cables*, with that almost-laugh underneath it, and the way she'd looked at him in the moment after he'd said the thing about *I've got you* — not the look he'd expected, not the formal, gracious acknowledgment. Something more private. Something that existed behind the public face of what she was.

He thought about that for a very long time.

He was in trouble, and he knew it, and he also knew that it was the least practical infatuation in the long history of impractical human infatuations, and he thought about that too, and it didn't help at all.

## Part Seven: Close Range

November.

They fell into a thing, he and Kara. He couldn't have named exactly when it began. It was accumulative, the way real things usually are.

It started with the AP History study group that Mr. Okonkwo recommended for the midterm — a vague suggestion that a few of them might benefit from meeting outside class, which most people ignored but which Marcus, Danny, a girl named Simone, and Kara all ended up participating in, meeting in the school library two afternoons a week. It was not warm at first. Danny and Simone had an established energy that Kara existed tangentially to, and Marcus wasn't sure where to put himself in relation to the quiet, precise girl with the books.

But here is what he found: Kara Danvers, in a small group with a concrete intellectual task, was completely different from Kara Danvers navigating a hallway or a cafeteria.

In the library, with the flash cards and the timeline sheets and the specific ergonomics of a round table that put everyone in each other's immediate vicinity, she was *present* in a way she hadn't been before. She was still quiet — she never competed for speaking time, never bulldozed the way some academically confident people did. But when she engaged, the engagement was complete. She asked questions that were exactly as sophisticated as her comments, which suggested she wasn't showing off in either direction — just thinking, genuinely, in real time.

And she was funny. That was the thing that surprised him most. Not obviously, loudly funny. A dry, sidelong funny. She'd said something one afternoon about the specific geopolitical miscalculations of World War One that made Danny laugh so hard he knocked his water bottle off the table, and then she'd looked slightly surprised by the response, as if she hadn't been certain the humor was going to land.

"You're actually funny," Marcus said to her, on the third meeting, after Danny and Simone had packed up and left and they were still finishing their notes.

She looked up. "Why 'actually'?"

"Because it took a while to notice. You don't lead with it."

"Neither do you," she said.

He considered this. "Fair."

"I don't lead with a lot of things," she said. She said it plainly, without self-pity, just as information. She was closing her notebooks, stacking them with that slightly over-precise care she had, and she wasn't looking at him.

"Why not?" he asked.

She was quiet for a moment. "It takes me a while to trust spaces," she said finally, and then seemed to hear the thing she'd said and close around it slightly. "I mean — I'm not — it's not—" She stopped. "I moved around a lot. New places were just always — new."

"Where did you move from?" he asked. Not prying. Genuinely curious.

"Far away," she said, and almost smiled. "Farther than it sounds."

He wanted to ask more. He didn't. He filed the moment away.

"You know what I keep thinking about?" he said instead. "The way you answered that question about the Korean War in week two. You talked about the concept of a limited war being *invented in real time*. I've been thinking about that phrase for weeks."

She looked at him more fully than she usually did. "Why?"

"Because it's interesting. To think about people living inside a concept before the concept has a name. Doing something without the vocabulary for it. I think that's — I think that's a real thing. I think that happens more than we notice."

Something happened in her expression. A very slight softening, somewhere around the eyes. "Yes," she said. "I think so too."

They walked out of the library side by side, neither of them in a particular hurry. The November afternoon was cold and bright, the kind that felt clean.

"Do you walk home?" she asked, at the building exit.

"Yeah. You?"

"Usually." She paused. "I go the Morrison Street way."

"I go Fifth," he said. "Which is the other direction."

"Yes," she said.

They stood at the door for a moment.

"See you Thursday," he said.

"See you Thursday," she said.

She walked away, and he watched her go for exactly as long as was reasonable and then slightly longer, and then turned and walked home.

---

He saw Supergirl again in mid-November.

It was a smaller thing than the bridge — a chemical spill at the industrial park on the south side, a tank car that had been improperly sealed, a plume of hazardous gas that needed to be contained before it reached the residential grid a mile downwind. He only saw it from a distance, from the ridge of the overpass where a group of onlookers had gathered. She was a small figure in blue and red against the gray industrial backdrop, a breath of cold from across the distance as her freeze breath did what it needed to do.

But at one point she rose above the site to survey the containment progress, and she was backlit by the low afternoon sun, and for just a moment she was suspended there — not moving, just present, looking outward at the city she watched over — and Marcus felt the same thing he'd felt on the bridge.

That private, un-performative devotion.

He thought about the girl in the library. The one who'd said *it takes me a while to trust spaces*. He thought about Supergirl saying *most people mention the cables*, with that hidden laugh. He thought about the way both of them had a quality of considering things fully before speaking. The way both of them seemed to operate with some significant part of themselves private, internal, available only in certain conditions.

He shook his head.

He was projecting. He was an idiot. He had developed feelings for a superhero and was now finding echoes of her in an ordinary girl who sat next to him in the library twice a week.

He was definitely going to think about this more, though. He was definitely going to keep doing that.

## Part Eight: The Almost

December.

The study group had drifted, as study groups do, past its original mandate. The midterm had been taken — Kara had gotten a 98, Marcus a 91, Danny an 84 and a long complaint about the essay question — and the meetings had continued anyway, converted by common unspoken agreement from test prep to the thing they'd actually been building toward, which was friendship.

They were in the library on a Wednesday afternoon in early December — just Marcus and Kara, Danny having a thing, Simone having another thing — and the work had been done for twenty minutes but neither of them had moved.

Kara was reading. Not a school book — the Sumerian primer was back, she'd produced it from her bag with the casualness of someone who reads Sumerian in their spare time, which was apparently a thing Kara Danvers did. Marcus was sketching in the margin of his notebook, the absent, not-really-drawing kind of sketching.

"Can I ask you something?" he said.

She looked up. "Okay."

"What is it like?" He tapped the primer. "Learning a new language. An old one."

She considered the question with that genuine consideration she brought to things. "Disorienting," she said. "Languages have — they have shapes. Like, not just rules, but a kind of structural *personality*. English is flexible and slightly chaotic. German is very organized. Ancient Sumerian is — it's fascinating because you can feel in the grammar how the people who made it thought. What they considered important enough to encode. What distinctions they found necessary."

"What distinctions did they find necessary?"

She smiled — a small one, looking at the book. "They had a word for the feeling of seeing a distant light and not knowing if it's a city or a star." She paused. "There isn't a word for that in English."

He thought about that. "There really isn't," he said.

"They had a lot of words for sky," she added. "Different kinds. Sky during rain, sky during drought, sky at the specific moment before sunrise. I think they must have spent a lot of time outside."

"Do you?" he asked. "Spend a lot of time outside?"

She looked at him. "Yes," she said, carefully.

"At night?"

Something shifted in her expression, briefly. "Sometimes," she said.

"Do you ever go up on the ridge?" he asked. "The east ridge, I mean. There's a spot—"

"Near the water tower," she said.

"You know it?"

"I've been there," she said, again with that care, that particular way she had of giving information in exactly the amount she'd decided on.

"The sky is remarkable from up there," he said.

She was quiet for a moment. Then: "Yes," she said. "It is."

He looked at her. Really looked, which he had trained himself not to do too obviously. The afternoon light from the library windows was doing something specific to her coloring — the gold of her hair, the exact shade of her eyes, that clear, serious, careful face.

He thought, involuntarily and with enough force that it felt like something physical: *she is actually beautiful.*

And then: *I am an idiot.*

And then, underneath both of those: *I wonder what she thinks about.*

"Can I ask you something now?" she said.

"Sure."

"The guitar."

He blinked. "What about it?"

"Are you any good?"

"No," he said, honestly. "I mean — I'm learning. I'm bad in a direction of being good, if that makes sense. The technique is there sometimes. The feel isn't always there."

"What do you play? When you're up there."

He went very still for a second. "Up where?"

"When you practice," she said, and something in her expression was very neutral, very calibrated, and he had the sudden disorienting sense of standing on a surface he'd thought was solid and finding it slightly less solid than he'd assumed. "I just meant — do you have a style you're working toward?"

"How do you know about the roof?" he said.

She was quiet for a moment. One moment too long.

"Becca mentioned it," she said. "She lives near you. She might have mentioned hearing someone practicing."

It was a reasonable explanation. It was even, he told himself, probably true.

But the way she'd said *when you're up there* before she'd corrected it to *when you practice* — that specific word, *there*, implying location, implying a specific knowledge of place—

He filed it. He didn't push.

"Mostly folk stuff," he said. "Some of my own stuff. Nothing finished."

"I'd like to hear it sometime," she said.

"You'd probably hear a lot of the same chord transition being attempted repeatedly."

"I wouldn't mind that," she said.

He looked at her. She looked at the Sumerian primer.

"Kara," he said.

She looked up.

He didn't say anything. He'd meant to say something, but the specific word he was looking for wasn't available at this particular moment, and so he just looked at her, and she looked at him, and it was December and the library was warm and outside the window the first snow of the year was beginning, quietly, without announcement.

"Never mind," he said.

"Okay," she said.

She looked back at her book. But she was smiling, slightly, in a way she probably thought he hadn't noticed.

He'd noticed.

## Part Nine: The Night Everything Got Harder

It was a Saturday night in mid-December when the thing happened that made everything more complicated.

Marcus was at Danny's house, a low-key gathering of six people watching a bad movie and eating chips, when the emergency alert went to everyone's phones simultaneously: *MAJOR INCIDENT - Downtown district - All non-essential personnel shelter in place*.

They went to the windows. You could see it from Danny's second floor — something happening in the downtown grid, six blocks north: a glow that wasn't normal light, a rising column of debris, and the particular sound of something structural failing.

"What is that?" Simone said.

Danny was already on his phone, pulling up the news. It came fast, the way news came now. The live feed was chaotic but the shape of it emerged: an explosion at the Harker Building — a twelve-story office complex, the result of what appeared to be a gas main failure amplified by a secondary structural issue. Parts of three floors had collapsed internally. There were people trapped.

And Supergirl was there.

They watched it on Danny's TV, the live news feed, a helicopter shot. She was moving through the building — not through the doors, but through the walls, in the precise surgical way, tearing openings for the emergency crews to bring people out. Every few minutes she emerged with someone, carried to the medical staging area on the street, and went back in.

Marcus sat on Danny's couch and watched and felt the familiar, helpless sensation of someone watching something happen that they have no way to participate in.

They all kept watching.

On the third-floor collapse, the helicopter cameras caught something that made everyone in Danny's living room go quiet. A section of floor gave way as she was making her way toward a group of trapped workers in the northeast corner — a chain failure, the structural supports under the already-weakened zone giving all at once. She fell two floors.

There was a moment on the feed where she was not visible. A long moment. Ten seconds, fifteen, twenty.

Marcus's hands were tight on his knees.

She came back out of the debris. Of course she did. She was Supergirl. She stood, shook dust from her cape, located the people she'd been moving toward through the walls, and continued.

But those twenty seconds.

He sat with those twenty seconds.

He thought about the woman in the library who'd said *it takes me a while to trust spaces*, and felt something he didn't know what to do with. A worry that was specific and personal, not the public kind.

---

She was fine.

Kara was always fine after things like this, in the specific physical sense. The fall had hurt, in the way that physical impacts on Earth still registered for her — a dull, large pain that faded within minutes, the Kryptonian biology repairing itself with efficiency that never stopped being slightly surreal to her. By the time she'd gotten everyone out — all fourteen people, not one casualty — she was fine.

She was not fine in the other sense.

She sat on the roof of the DEO facility at midnight, wrapped in a blanket someone had given her, and felt the weight of the evening distribute itself through her body. This was always the part that no one filmed, no one reported. The after. The sitting with it. The specific exhaustion of spending the entire capacity of what you are for two solid hours, and the particular kind of aloneness that came after, when the emergency had passed and the city was returning to its regular noise and you were just a girl on a roof in the cold.

Alex came and sat beside her.

"You did good," Alex said.

"I know," Kara said. Which was not arrogance. It was just true, and Kara had learned to say the true things to her sister without the softening that she applied everywhere else.

"Everyone's out."

"I know."

Alex put an arm around her. Kara leaned her head on her sister's shoulder, which she only ever did when she was genuinely tired, the deep kind.

"I keep thinking," Kara said, "about the afterward. For them. For the people who were in there. They're going to think about it for years. Some of them."

"Yes," Alex said.

"I can't — I can't fix the afterward. I can only fix the emergency."

"That's right."

"Sometimes I wish I could do the other thing too."

Alex was quiet for a moment. "You do do the other thing too, sometimes. You just don't get to see it."

Kara thought about this.

She thought about a boy on a roof playing guitar. She thought about a library window with snow starting outside. She thought about *most people mention the cables* and the quality of his laugh when she'd said it.

She thought about how close those two parts of her life — the human part, the careful, trying-to-be-ordinary part, and the cape-and-crisis part — were to touching each other, and how much she had built to keep them separate, and how the separation felt, lately, like something that required more effort than it used to.

---

## Part Ten: Truth in Layers

January.

After winter break — which Kara had spent partly at the Danvers house with Eliza and Alex, a Christmas that was warm in all the ways Christmas should be and some that were specifically and peculiarly alien, because Eliza Danvers always found a way to work Kryptonian traditions into the holiday when she knew enough to do it — the spring semester began.

Something had shifted between Marcus and Kara. They both felt it, operated around it without directly acknowledging it, the way you navigate furniture in a dark room that you've learned by feel.

They still met in the library — not for study group now, just the two of them, the pretense of studying having been dropped. They just met and read in each other's company and talked, which was its own thing, its own newly minted category.

He had started to understand the architecture of her.

She was careful, not timid. There was a difference. Timidity was the avoidance of exposure because you doubted your own value. Kara's carefulness was something else — it felt like the behavior of someone who had learned, concretely and specifically, that exposure had consequences, and was managing those consequences with intelligence rather than fear.

She was attentive in a way that made him feel, when he was talking to her, that he was being genuinely heard. Not heard-politely. Heard the way information is really heard, processed, considered.

She sometimes went still in the middle of a conversation in a way that he'd started to recognize as the thing she did before she said something real. A kind of preparation.

He liked her. Specifically, thoroughly, increasingly urgently. He had stopped pretending to himself that this was complicated by the Supergirl feeling, that the two things were in competition. He had, reluctantly and then completely, admitted to himself that the feeling had become one feeling, belonging to one person. He wasn't sure how. He wasn't sure it mattered.

He had not said anything. He was not going to say anything until he was sure of the ground under his feet.

---

She was keeping track of what she told him.

Not deceptively — or not only deceptively. More like building a map of what was true in the Kara Danvers shape of her life, the edges of what she could offer. She had told him: that she'd moved around. That she liked knowing things. That she found certain languages interesting in the way they encoded cognition. That she found social situations generally exhausting and intellectually somewhat under-stimulating. That she had a sister she was close to. That she thought about the sky more than most people did.

These were all completely true.

She had not told him: that she could hear his heartbeat from twelve feet away, and that it had a very specific and, she found, affecting rhythm that she had memorized involuntarily. That she knew from the sky above his roof what a Thursday night sounded like at his house. That when she thought about the levee in the rain, the thing she thought about most was not the levee.

She had not told him: *I've got you*. Three words. The private ones.

She was also, around January, beginning to notice something.

He kept looking at the sky.

Not the sky in general — the sky at moments when, if someone were watching closely, there might be something to see. A small sonic artifact at altitude. A streak of movement in the cloud cover. The particular nothing that was left when someone moving very fast had just passed through it.

He was doing the thing that occasionally very attentive people did, which was assembling the arithmetic of her life without knowing that was what they were doing.

She noticed this. She catalogued it.

She was not alarmed by it in the way she should have been. She was alarmed by the fact that she was not alarmed by it. She was alarmed by the specific warmth she felt when he looked at the sky.

## Part Eleven: The Ridge

It happened in February, on a day that started cold and went colder.

They had been talking, over the course of several weeks, about the east ridge and the water tower, in the way they talked about most things — obliquely, approaching it from different directions, the topic surfacing and submerging. He'd suggested once, with the particular casualness that indicated it was not casual, that they should go up there sometime.

She had said, with the particular neutrality that indicated it was not neutral, that they should.

February 4th was a Saturday with no wind and a sky so clear it felt like it had been specifically cleaned for viewing. He texted her at noon: *East ridge. 2pm. Unless you have plans.*

She considered the text for a long time. She was, technically, on call. She was always, technically, on call. Alex could reach her. The city could reach her.

She texted back: *2pm. I'll be there.*

She was there at 1:58, which was two minutes before him, because she did not take the bus or walk.

She had landed, silently and invisibly, on the back side of the ridge, changed out of the suit in the small storage space she'd established there months ago, and was sitting on the rock outcropping near the water tower, boots on the stone, looking out at the city, when she heard his footsteps on the trail.

She had been looking at the city for two minutes and had been thinking, as she did from this specific vantage point, about the way the aerial view and the ground view were both true simultaneously. The city looked like one thing from up here. It was a thousand things from inside.

"You're early," Marcus said, slightly out of breath from the trail.

"So are you," she said.

He sat on the rock beside her, not too close but close enough. He had his jacket zipped up and his terrible hair doing its wind-lifted thing, and he was looking out at the city below with that expression she'd catalogued — the fully-present, no-performance expression.

"I used to come up here a lot in middle school," he said. "When things were weird at home. I'd just come up here and look at it."

"What was weird at home?"

"My dad left when I was twelve." He said it without excessive weight. Not performing resilience, not performing wound. Just saying it, plainly. "It wasn't dramatic. He just — gradually wasn't there, and then he definitively wasn't there. My mom handled it well. I handled it less well, privately."

"I'm sorry," she said.

"It's okay now. I'm telling you because—" He paused. "Because I told you something and it seems fair."

"I didn't tell you anything that specific."

"No," he agreed. "But you told me about the spaces. Trusting them. That was specific."

She was quiet.

"Where did you come from?" he asked. Not pushingly. Just finally asking the thing he'd been not-asking.

"Somewhere with a different sky," she said.

He looked at her.

"I know that sounds—" She stopped. "I mean — the climate was different. Where I grew up. Before the Danvers. It was somewhere very — the sky had a different color. Not dramatically different. A little warmer in the blue." She was treading a line, she knew, a line between technically true and true. "I still miss it sometimes."

"Do you have any family there?"

Her hands were on her knees. "No," she said. "Not anymore."

He understood, from the specific quality of the silence, not to ask more. "I'm sorry," he said.

"It's okay," she said, echoing him, and it came out slightly softer than she'd intended.

They sat in the cold, clear afternoon, and below them Lakewood was laid out in its ordinary complexity — streets and rooftops and the winding thread of the Calloway, the smoke of industry on the south end, the green space of the park cutting through the eastern grid.

"I can see where the bridge was from here," Marcus said.

"Can you?"

"There." He pointed. She didn't need to look in the direction he was pointing; she knew exactly where every structure in this city was. "Where they've got the repair scaffolding. You can just see it from here if you know where to look."

"Were you there?" she asked, carefully. "When it happened?"

"Yeah. I was walking. Heard the sirens." He was still looking at the bridge. "I saw her."

"What was it like?" She asked the question quietly, looking out at the city. Not at him.

"Have you ever seen something and not been able to make it fit into your existing—" He searched. "Your existing understanding of scale? Like, not just big, but *different*. A different category."

"Yes," she said.

"It was like that." He was quiet for a moment. "I talked to her. After the levee. Last October."

Kara was very still. "Did you?"

"I told her—" He stopped. "I told her that the thing that mattered wasn't the physical part of what she did. That it was the way she spoke to the people she was saving."

"What did she say?"

"She said most people mention the cables."

And there it was.

Three seconds.

That was how long it took — three seconds of absolute silence, during which Kara understood exactly what was happening and felt the world make a specific sound she had no name for and held herself very, very carefully still.

He hadn't heard his own words, she thought. He didn't know what he'd just said.

"She sounds—" Kara said, and her voice was almost steady. "That sounds like a person worth knowing."

He turned and looked at her then. Really looked. The full, amber-brown, amber-in-full-sun gaze that she had catalogued and tried not to catalogue.

"Yeah," he said. "She does."

Something in his voice was different. Something was in his voice that she didn't know what to do with, and neither, from the look of him, did he.

"Kara," he said.

"Yes."

"I have been — I have not been good at saying the things I want to say recently." He looked at his hands, then back at her. "And I think it's because the thing I want to say is a lot of things and they're organized in a way that isn't — simple. And I don't want to say the simple version of something complicated and have it be wrong."

"Tell me the complicated version," she said.

He breathed in. Cold air, February air. "I think about you constantly," he said. "Not in a straightforward way. In a — I think about something you said in the library and then I think about — something else, someone else, an impression of someone else, and then I think about you again and there's something that—" He stopped. "This is coming out wrong."

"It's not," she said.

"There's something," he said more slowly, "that I feel when I'm around you that I've only felt in one other context, and I can't explain how those two things are the same and so I've been sitting with that confusion for months. And I don't know what to do with it."

Kara looked at the city below them. She thought about all the things she was. She thought about the suit in the storage space on the back of the ridge. She thought about the sound of his guitar, heard from three hundred feet above, and the way she'd slowed down, and stayed.

She thought about Alex saying *you don't have to be that invisible*.

She thought about the word she'd told him in Sumerian: the word for seeing a distant light and not knowing if it's a city or a star.

And she thought about trust, and its weight, and what it meant to set it down.

"Marcus," she said.

"Yeah."

"I have to tell you something." Her voice was quiet and precise, the way her voice was when she was about to say a true thing. "And I need you to just — I need you to let me say the whole thing before you react."

He looked at her. "Okay."

"The reason that feels the same," she said, "is that it *is* the same." A pause. The city below them. The cold, clean sky. "It's me. Both of it. It's me."

Silence.

He was very still. She watched him process it — watched the sequence of responses cross his face without performance, without concealment, because that was the kind of person he was: the first response of *that can't be* followed by the immediate interrogation of the past months, the things that hadn't quite fit, the specific knowledge of the guitar on the roof, the way she'd said *when you're up there*, the word *there*, the exact color of both pairs of eyes.

He looked at her eyes.

"Your eyes," he said.

"Yes," she said.

"Both of you — both of your—"

"Yes."

"The Sumerian," he said. "You learned it because—"

"Language encodes what people think matters," she said. "And Krypton had a language too. Sometimes I look for it in other old things." She stopped. "I'm from Krypton. I'm Kryptonian. I've been on Earth since I was twelve. The Danvers took me in. The rest of it — the suit, the work — that started two years ago. I didn't choose this face or this identity to — I didn't do it to deceive anyone. I did it to protect people. To protect myself, and the people around me." She looked at him very steadily. "I'm telling you because I think you've already half-figured it out and because—" She stopped.

"Because what?" he said softly.

"Because I don't want to keep having the secret between us," she said. "I don't want to keep being — two things to you. I want to be one thing."

He was quiet for a long time. The light was changing, the winter afternoon sliding toward gold, the city turning amber below.

"Say something," she said.

"I'm thinking," he said.

She waited.

"On the ridge," he said finally, "two months ago. You were already there when I arrived. Two minutes early."

"Yes."

"You didn't walk up. Or take the bus."

"No."

"Okay." He breathed out. "Okay." He was quiet again. Then: "The guitar. The roof. You heard it from—"

"From above," she said. "I was on patrol. I slowed down."

"You slowed down."

"Yes."

The amber in his eyes was very clear in the low winter light. "Because?"

She looked at the city. "Because it was beautiful," she said. "The way you kept trying the same thing until it was right. I wanted to hear it be right."

The longest silence.

Then: "I caught your book," he said. "The orbital mechanics one. In September."

"Yes."

"You could have caught it yourself."

"Yes."

"Why didn't you?"

She thought about this. "Because," she said carefully, "I wanted to see what you would do."

He looked at her. She looked back.

He laughed — not the expected response, but it was his laugh, the genuine one, and it broke something that had been very tightly held in the air between them for a long time.

"I caught a falling book," he said. "That was my — that was the audition."

"You passed," she said.

He was still smiling. The smile became quieter, became the private one. "Kara."

"Yes."

"I was going to say something about how you can't get hypothermia," he said. "In the rain. You told me to take care of myself."

"You were soaked."

"You were perfectly dry when you arrived. It had been raining for two hours."

"I arrived quickly," she said.

"You arrived from the sky."

"Yes."

"From my roof."

"From near your roof. I had been near your roof." A pause. "I wasn't — I don't patrol your roof."

"You heard the guitar from above."

"I happened to be—"

"Kara."

She stopped. He was looking at her with the full, steady, amber gaze. Not challenging. Just present. Just asking her to be there with him.

"Yes," she said. "From near your roof. I slowed down."

"To hear the guitar."

"To hear you."

The city was very quiet below them, or everything else was very quiet below them, and the late afternoon was going golden-orange, the particular light of winter ending, and she was aware, with senses she never fully switched off, of his heartbeat — the strong, specific, familiar rhythm that she had memorized without meaning to — and it was doing something different than usual, and she thought hers probably was too, though she had never been entirely sure her biology did exactly what his did.

"I was in love with two people," he said. "And they were the same person."

"Yes," she said.

"That's the most absurd thing that has ever happened to me."

"It's fairly unusual from my side too."

"Is it?" He tilted his head. "Has anyone ever—"

"No," she said. "Not like this."

"How did they usually—"

"Usually they saw Supergirl and felt the thing they felt and looked right through Kara Danvers, because she was quiet and careful and she had her hair up." She paused. "You kept looking at both of us."

"Both of you are the same," he said. "I kept seeing the same thing in both of you, and I couldn't explain it."

"What were you seeing?"

He thought about it for a long moment. The honest version. "Someone who was paying attention to something that most people weren't paying attention to," he said. "Both times. Whatever the situation was — the bridge, the library, wherever — you were somewhere in it fully, in a way most people weren't. Both of you." He stopped. "Both of you, who are the same you."

The last of the sun was going now. The city lights were coming on below, individually at first, then in their grids, the map of Lakewood reassembling itself in amber and white.

She could see, from here, the east levee. The bridge. The Harker Building with its temporary supports, still under repair.

She could see every place she'd been needed, every place the world had required something of her, laid out below her in the geography of this city that was, she had understood for a while now, her city. The one she had chosen and been chosen by.

She felt his hand, careful and questioning, settle next to hers on the rock. Not taking it. Just placing itself beside it, in proximity, in suggestion.

She looked at his hand.

She looked at the city.

She looked at him.

"Marcus," she said.

"Yeah."

"I can't — I need you to understand what this means. The secret. If you know who I am — I can't unknow it. You can't. And there are people who would use what you know. Who would—"

"I know," he said. His voice was very steady. "I know what I'm saying yes to."

"I haven't asked you anything yet."

"You're telling me the thing you're about to ask," he said. "Whether it matters to me. Whether it changes it. Whether I can hold the weight of it." He paused. "The answer is yes to all three."

She studied his face. She was very good at reading faces — at reading the small physiological tells that indicated internal state, the microexpressions, the rate and quality of breathing, the things people didn't know they were broadcasting. She had long ago learned to stop using most of this, because it felt like cheating in the context of ordinary human relationships. She used it now, fully, and what she found was this: he was afraid. He was slightly, honestly afraid. And he was telling her yes anyway.

Which was, she thought, the only version of yes worth anything.

She turned her hand over, palm up.

He placed his hand in hers.

Below them, Lakewood breathed its evening breath, ten thousand ordinary stories unfolding in the amber light, none of them this story, none of them two people on a ridge at the end of winter, finding in each other the thing they hadn't had a word for until now.

---

## Epilogue: Morning Sky

March.

Marcus was on the roof when he heard the sound — familiar now, the particular hush of displaced air, the absence that indicated a fast arrival.

She landed behind him, quiet as a thought.

She wasn't in the suit. She was in jeans and a white sweater, her hair down, which she was doing more often lately, and she had two cups of coffee from the place on Morrison that she'd learned he liked, which meant she had either walked twelve minutes at human pace or flown thirty seconds and landed around the corner.

He suspected the latter.

"You're early," he said.

"I wanted to see the sunrise," she said.

She sat beside him on the flat roof. She gave him one of the coffees. Below, Lakewood was waking up, the first pale light edging over the eastern ridge, the particular blue of pre-dawn giving way to the specific, unrepeatable pink of this morning specifically.

He watched the light change.

She watched the sky with an expression that she no longer tried to hide — the one that was between longing and belonging, between the lost world and the found one, between the girl she had been and the girl she was becoming, in this city, under this yellow sun, next to this person.

He reached over and took her hand.

She looked at him.

"Morning," he said.

"Morning," she said.

Above them, the sky was going from pink to gold, and it was ordinary, and it was extraordinary, and it was theirs.
